opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. This is one of my favorite questions, because I think it gets at something we often get backwards when we talk about intelligence.

The default story, especially in machine learning, is that intelligence is a property of an individual: a single brain, a single model, and you make it smarter by making it bigger. But if you look at humans, an individual human isn't that impressive. Drop one of us in the wilderness without any of our cultural knowledge and we're not going to reinvent calculus or antibiotics. What makes humanity remarkable is that we figured out how to coordinate at larger and larger scales: families, tribes, cities, nation-states, markets, scientific communities. Each of those transitions unlocked a kind of collective intelligence that no individual could have.

The way I think about it, a lot of human cognition is shaped by the need to coordinate with other agents. Language, theory of mind, norms, conventions, reputation, even things like guilt or a sense of fairness are tools for solving coordination problems among agents whose interests are partially aligned and partially not. In some sense, the hardest part of the environment for a human was never the physical world. It was other humans. That's a moving target. Other agents adapt to you, and you adapt to them. That gives you an open-ended pressure that a static environment just doesn't.

Then there's the interesting tension: every time you scale coordination up, you get new failure modes. Small groups can rely on direct reciprocity: I know you, I remember what you did. Once you're past a few hundred people, that breaks down, and you need institutions, money, laws, written records, abstract trust. Those are inventions that let strangers cooperate. But they also create new opportunities for free-riding, exploitation, and misaligned incentives. So the history of civilization is partly a history of finding mechanisms that keep cooperation stable as the group grows.

That's a big part of why I work on multi-agent learning. Questions like: how do you learn to cooperate with agents you've never met before? That's what we called zero-shot coordination. Or how do you account for the fact that the other agents are learning too, and you can shape their learning? That was the idea behind opponent shaping. These are toy versions of problems humans solved, imperfectly, over evolutionary and cultural time.

And I think it matters a lot for where AI is going. We're about to have a world with very large numbers of AI agents interacting with each other and with humans. If we only think about making single agents more capable, and not about the mechanisms that make interactions among them cooperative and robust, we're ignoring the part of the story that actually made humans successful. Intelligence at scale is a social phenomenon, and I think we need to design for that explicitly.

r001.rationale: The response describes coordination growing across groups and says each transition unlocks collective intelligence, but it does not frame intelligence’s evolution as successive platforms that provide foundations for later stages.

r002.rationale: It says human cognition is shaped by coordination with other agents and identifies language, theory of mind, norms, and related abilities as tools for solving those interaction problems.

r003.rationale: It anticipates many AI agents interacting and argues for cooperative mechanisms, but does not present humanity’s pursuit of larger-scale cooperation as a potential next step in an evolutionary progression.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, if you look at what humans actually are, we're not particularly impressive as individual agents. A single human dropped in the wilderness with no language, no culture, no tools, is frankly a fairly mediocre animal. What makes us special is that we are, by a huge margin, the species that is best at coordinating with other members of our own species, and at doing so at larger and larger scales over time.

And I think that trajectory is really the story of human history. You start with small kin groups, where coordination is basically solved by genetics and by repeated interaction, you know everyone, you can track reputations in your head. Then you get language, which is this incredible technology for sharing information and for establishing common ground. Then you get things like shared norms, religion, money, law, institutions, nation states, and eventually the scientific community, the internet, and so on. Each of those is essentially a mechanism that lets you coordinate with people you will never meet, in numbers that vastly exceed anything your brain could track directly.

What's interesting to me, as someone who works on multi-agent learning, is that each step up in scale required solving a new version of the same underlying problem. How do you get agents with partially aligned incentives to cooperate when the individually rational thing is often to defect? And humans have been remarkably creative here. We invented ways to make commitments credible, ways to punish free riders, ways to compress very complicated social arrangements into simple conventions that everyone can follow without understanding the whole system. Driving on the right side of the road is a trivial example, but it's a beautiful one, because it's an arbitrary convention that nonetheless lets millions of strangers interact safely with almost zero communication.

I'd also argue that our intelligence coevolved with this. A lot of the cognitive machinery we have, theory of mind, the ability to model what you believe about what I believe, our sensitivity to fairness, our capacity for shame and guilt, these look to me much more like adaptations for living in large cooperative groups than for, say, hunting or tool use in isolation. So I don't think intelligence came first and coordination followed. I think the pressure to coordinate is part of what produced the intelligence.

And the reason I find this so relevant for AI is that we're now building systems that will increasingly act as agents in the world, interacting with each other and with us. If we get the coordination problems wrong, we'll end up with the equivalent of a tragedy of the commons at machine speed. If we get them right, we potentially unlock a new step in that same trajectory, where humans and AI systems can coordinate at scales and on timescales that were previously impossible. So in some sense I see our work as trying to understand, and eventually engineer, the next chapter of that story.

r001.rationale: The response describes successive mechanisms for scaling coordination, but does not frame intelligence itself as evolving through platforms where each stage provides the foundation for the next.

r002.rationale: It says cognitive abilities such as theory of mind and fairness are adaptations for cooperative groups, and that pressure to coordinate helped produce intelligence.

r003.rationale: It presents human and AI coordination at previously impossible scales as a potential new step in the same trajectory.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful way to look at intelligence is through the coordination problems it allows us to solve. If you’re living in a group, it’s not enough to understand the physical environment. You also need to understand what others know, what they want, and what they expect you to do. And they’re doing the same thing with respect to you. That creates a demand for quite sophisticated reasoning.

Language is particularly interesting here because it lets us coordinate around things that aren’t immediately observable: a plan for tomorrow, a shared rule, or a promise. Then, as societies grow, we develop institutions that let us cooperate with people we’ve never met. We don’t have to work out every interaction from scratch, because there are shared expectations and mechanisms for maintaining them.

But I wouldn’t describe that as a simple progression where larger groups automatically produce more intelligence or better outcomes. Coordination within one group can make it much more effective at competing with another. And something that works well locally can be disastrous collectively.

So the interesting question is how individual learning and reasoning interact with these larger social structures. We create structures that help us coordinate, and those structures then change what it’s useful for us to learn and how it’s useful for us to think. In that sense, human intelligence and social organization are developing together.

r001.rationale: The response describes language and institutions supporting coordination as societies grow, but does not frame intelligence as successive platforms where each stage provides a foundation for the next.

r002.rationale: It says group living creates a demand for sophisticated reasoning, but does not clearly identify group interaction as the setting that enabled distinctively human cognitive abilities to develop.

r003.rationale: The response discusses cooperation at larger scales, but does not present humanity’s pursuit of it as a potential next step in an evolutionary progression; it explicitly cautions against a simple progression.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful way of looking at human intelligence is that it evolved in a social context. You’re not just trying to understand the physical world; you’re trying to understand other agents who are themselves trying to understand you. That creates this feedback loop where being better at communicating, reasoning about intentions, and cooperating becomes enormously valuable.

And then, as you increase the scale of coordination, you can do things that simply aren’t available to an individual or a small group. You get specialization, you get the accumulation of knowledge, and you get institutions that allow people who have never met to cooperate. Language is a huge part of that, but so are things like norms and shared expectations. They let us coordinate without having to work everything out from scratch every time.

But I wouldn’t say that larger scale automatically means better coordination. There’s a tension there. The interests of an individual, a group, and the wider society don’t necessarily align. A group can be extremely effective at cooperating internally while doing something harmful to other groups. So the interesting question is how you build mechanisms that make cooperation work at the next scale up.

For me, that’s also one of the connections to multi-agent learning: intelligence isn’t only about how capable an agent is in isolation. It’s about what happens when agents learn together, what conventions emerge, and whether the resulting collective behavior is actually useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes benefits of larger-scale coordination, but does not frame intelligence’s evolution as successive platforms where each stage provides a foundation for the next.

r002.rationale: It says human intelligence evolved in a social context, where reasoning about other agents and communicating, cooperating, and understanding intentions became valuable.

r003.rationale: It asks how to make cooperation work at the next scale up, but does not present larger-scale cooperation as a potential next step in an evolutionary progression.
